items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium that has risen from 5.0 mmol/L to 6.8 mmol/L (5.0 to 6.8 mEq/L) over 2 days. Which change on the cardiac monitor is typically the EARLIEST ECG sign of this electrolyte imbalance?

options.text: Prominent U waves following flattened T waves
Tall, narrow, peaked T waves
A prolonged QT interval
A sine-wave pattern

rationales.A: Incorrect. Flattened or depressed T waves with prominent U waves are the ECG pattern of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
rationales.B: Correct. As potassium rises, tall, symmetric, peaked T waves are usually the first visible ECG change; with further increases the PR interval lengthens, the P wave disappears and the QRS widens.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperkalemia tends to shorten, not lengthen, the QT interval. A prolonged QT interval is characteristic of severe hypocalcemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A sine-wave pattern is a late, pre-arrest finding that appears after QRS widening, just before ventricular fibrillation or asystole; it is not the earliest sign.

items.topic: Hyperkalemia — ECG progression
items.units_note: Potassium in mmol/L is numerically equal to mEq/L.

sources.title: Hyperkalemia
sources.supports: Key B; rationales C (QT shortening) and D (sine wave is the final stage)
sources.evidence: ECG changes often visible when K > 5.5 mmol/L; tall, symmetric, peaked T waves initially; >6.5 mmol/L widened QRS, loss of P wave; finally sine wave then VF/asystole; QT shortening.

sources.title: 10.3 Electrolyte Imbalance (Table 10.7 Hypokalemia and Hyperkalemia)
sources.supports: Key B (tall, peaked T waves in hyperkalemia)
sources.evidence: Hyperkalemia clinical manifestations: tall, peaked T waves, widened QRS complex, prolonged PR interval.

sources.title: Hypokalemia
sources.evidence: Hypokalemia causes ST sagging, T-wave depression and U-wave elevation; T wave shrinks and U wave enlarges as it worsens.

sources.title: Hypocalcemia
sources.evidence: Severe hypocalcemia typically shows prolongation of the QTc and ST intervals.

Note: OpenStax Table 10.7 also lists U waves under hyperkalemia, which conflicts with Merck; that disputed detail is not keyed — U waves are used only as the hypokalemia distractor, supported by Merck.

items.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who uses insulin reports feeling shaky and sweaty 2 hours before lunch. The client is alert and able to swallow. Capillary blood glucose is 3.1 mmol/L (56 mg/dL). For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Give 15 g of carbohydrate as glucose tablets.
Recheck the capillary blood glucose 15 minutes after treatment.
Administer glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly.
Give a second 15 g of carbohydrate immediately, before any recheck, to prevent recurrence.
After the hypoglycemia resolves, offer a snack containing carbohydrate and protein because lunch is more than 1 hour away.

rationales.R1: Indicated. Mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia in a conscious adult is treated with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate; Diabetes Canada prefers glucose or sucrose tablets or solution.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Blood glucose is retested about 15 minutes after treatment, and another 15 g is given only if it is still low (Diabetes Canada: below 4.0 mmol/L).
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Glucagon 1 mg SC/IM is reserved for severe hypoglycemia when the person cannot take oral carbohydrate (for example, is unconscious) and IV access is not available. This client is alert and can swallow.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Re-treatment depends on the 15-minute recheck. Giving extra carbohydrate without rechecking risks overtreatment, which can cause rebound hyperglycemia and weight gain.
rationales.R5: Indicated. Once hypoglycemia is reversed, a snack with about 15 g of carbohydrate plus a protein source is recommended when the next meal is more than 1 hour away, to prevent recurrence.

items.topic: Hypoglycemia management in a conscious adult (rule of 15)
items.jurisdiction_note: Diabetes Canada defines hypoglycemia (insulin/secretagogue users) as plasma glucose <4.0 mmol/L and re-treats if still <4.0; Merck (US) uses <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) and re-treats if not >4.4 mmol/L (80 mg/dL). The stem value (3.1 mmol/L) is low under both, and the threshold difference is not tested.
items.units_note: Glucose 3.1 mmol/L × 18 ≈ 56 mg/dL.

sources.title: Hypoglycemia (Clinical Practice Guidelines, Chapter 14)
sources.source_date: 2018 CPG (Can J Diabetes 2018;42 Suppl 1) — no later revision shown on page
sources.evidence: Mild-moderate: 15 g carbohydrate, preferably glucose or sucrose tablets/solution; retest in 15 min, re-treat if <4.0 mmol/L; avoid overtreatment; snack with 15 g carb + protein if meal >1 h away; unconscious without IV: glucagon 1 mg SC/IM.

sources.title: Hypoglycemia
sources.section: Treatment in patients taking antihyperglycemic medications
sources.evidence: Rule of 15s: 15 g glucose or sucrose, recheck at 15 minutes; then a snack with complex carbohydrate and protein; glucagon 1 mg SC/IM (≥25 kg) for those unable to eat or drink.

items.stem: In an Ontario hospital, a 79-year-old client has been found incapable with respect to a proposed surgical treatment. The client's spouse, adult son, and sister are at the bedside. The chart contains a valid power of attorney for personal care that appoints the client's niece and gives her authority over treatment decisions. The niece is capable, available, and willing to act. Under Ontario law, who is the appropriate substitute decision-maker to give or refuse consent for this treatment?

options.text: The client's spouse
The client's niece
The client's adult son
The Public Guardian and Trustee

rationales.A: Incorrect. Under the Health Care Consent Act, 1996, a spouse or partner ranks below an attorney for personal care whose power of attorney covers treatment decisions.
rationales.B: Correct. An attorney for personal care with authority over treatment ranks above a spouse, children and siblings in the Act's list of substitute decision-makers. Because the niece is capable, available and willing, consent is obtained from her as the highest-ranked substitute decision-maker.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A child of the incapable person ranks below both the attorney for personal care and the spouse.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Public Guardian and Trustee decides only as a last resort, when no one on the list meets the requirements to act. A qualified attorney for personal care is available here.

items.topic: Consent — substitute decision-maker hierarchy (HCCA s. 20)
items.jurisdiction_note: Ranking set by Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, 1996, s. 20 (guardian; attorney for personal care; Board-appointed representative; spouse/partner; child or parent; parent with access only; sibling; other relative; PGT as last resort). Other provinces and US states use different surrogate laws; NCLEX items generally use generic advance-directive/health care proxy wording.

sources.title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 2, Sched. A
sources.section: s. 20(1) list of persons who may give or refuse consent; s. 20(2) requirements; s. 20(5) Public Guardian and Trustee

sources.supports: Key B; rationales A, C, D
sources.evidence: s.20(1): 1 guardian; 2 attorney for personal care; 3 Board-appointed representative; 4 spouse/partner; 5 child or parent; 7 brother/sister. s.20(5): PGT decides if no listed person meets s.20(2).

sources.title: Consent (Practice Guideline)

sources.supports: Key B (highest-ranked available, willing SDM); rationale D (PGT last resort)
sources.evidence: If incapable, consent is obtained from the highest ranked available substitute decision-maker from the HCCA hierarchy who is willing; the PGT is the substitute decision-maker of last resort.

items.stem: A client admitted to a medical unit has had a productive cough for 3 weeks with night sweats and weight loss, and active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which measures should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
Wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 respirator when entering the room.
Keep the room door closed whether or not the client is in the room.
Have the client wear a mask if transport out of the room is necessary.
Wear a surgical mask instead of a respirator, because tuberculosis spreads by large droplets.
Allow staff who report a previous tuberculosis infection to enter without a respirator.

rationales.A: Correct. Suspected or confirmed pulmonary or laryngeal TB requires Airborne Precautions in a single airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
rationales.B: Correct. Staff entering the room of a client with suspected active pulmonary TB must wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 (or higher) respirator.
rationales.C: Correct. The door of an airborne isolation room must stay closed to keep the negative-pressure air flow working; Ontario's PIDAC guidance says it is kept closed whether or not the client is in the room.
rationales.D: Correct. Transport out of the room is limited to what is necessary, and the client wears a mask during transport (if tolerated) for source control.
rationales.E: Incorrect. TB spreads by the airborne route in small droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air. A surgical mask does not reliably protect the wearer from inhaling them; an N95 respirator is the minimum.
rationales.F: Incorrect. The N95 requirement for active pulmonary TB applies to all staff. Immunity-based exceptions in Ontario's precautions apply to diseases such as measles and varicella, not TB.

items.jurisdiction_note: Keyed measures agree between Ontario PIDAC and US CDC. One known difference is NOT tested: PIDAC also requires transport staff to wear an N95 for active TB, whereas CDC says transport staff need no mask/respirator if the client is masked.

items.stem: A client with heart failure and peripheral edema has an order for furosemide 40 mg IV now. The vial is labelled furosemide injection 10 mg/mL. How many millilitres should the nurse prepare? Round to the nearest whole number.

rationales.calculation: Volume = dose ordered ÷ concentration = 40 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 4 mL. Check: 4 mL × 10 mg/mL = 40 mg. The dose is within the usual initial adult IV dose for edema in the Canadian product monograph and US labelling (20 to 40 mg as a single dose), and IV furosemide is given slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.

items.stem: After removing gloves following a routine bed bath, a nurse's hands are not visibly soiled. According to Ontario PIDAC hand-hygiene guidance (concordant with CDC clinical safety guidance), which action is preferred?

options.text: Wash with soap and running water for at least 2 minutes.
Apply a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub and rub until dry.
Rinse briefly with water only; no product is needed after glove removal.
Apply a non-alcohol waterless antiseptic foam as first choice.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Soap and water is required when hands are visibly soiled (or in certain spore-related situations). When hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based hand rub is preferred.
rationales.B: Correct. When hands are not visibly soiled, a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method in Ontario health-care settings and is also preferred by CDC in most clinical situations.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is still required after glove removal; rinsing with water alone is not an accepted method.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Non-alcohol-based waterless antiseptic agents are not recommended for hand hygiene in health-care settings.

items.stem: A nurse finishes care for a client with laboratory-confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection, removes gloves and gown, and finds a dedicated hand-washing sink immediately available. Hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand-hygiene method is preferred in this situation?

options.text: Apply alcohol-based hand rub only, because hands are not visibly soiled.
Wash with soap and water at the dedicated sink.
Wash with soap and water at the client's bathroom sink for convenience.
Skip hand hygiene because Contact Precautions gloves already protected the hands.

rationales.A: Incorrect. For C. difficile, soap and water is theoretically more effective at removing spores than alcohol-based hand rub when a dedicated sink is available.
rationales.B: Correct. PIDAC advises that when C. difficile is diagnosed or suspected and a dedicated hand-washing sink is immediately available, hands should be washed with soap and water. CDC likewise recommends soap and water during care of clients with C. difficile in outbreak settings.
rationales.C: Incorrect. PIDAC specifically advises not to perform hand hygiene at the client's sink because that may re-contaminate the health-care provider's hands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Meticulous hand hygiene is required after glove removal; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

items.jurisdiction_note: PIDAC prefers soap/water when a dedicated sink is available for C. difficile; if no dedicated sink, ABHR is used. The stem specifies a dedicated sink so the Canada-preferred action is keyed.

items.stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds intact skin over a client's sacral bony prominence with a localized area of nonblanchable erythema. Sensation over the area is slightly increased compared with surrounding skin. How should this finding be documented?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
Deep-tissue pressure injury

rationales.A: Correct. Stage 1 is intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema, often over a bony prominence; changes in sensation, temperature, or firmness may accompany it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Stage 2 involves partial-thickness skin loss (shallow open ulcer or blister) with a pink/red wound bed, not intact skin alone.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Unstageable injuries have full-thickness loss obscured by slough or eschar so depth cannot be determined.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Deep-tissue pressure injury presents as persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, not simple nonblanchable erythema of Stage 1.

items.stem: A client is confined to bed after major abdominal surgery and is assessed as high risk for pressure injury. Which repositioning schedule best reflects evidence-based pressure-reduction practice?

options.text: Turn the client at least every 2 hours using a written schedule.
Turn the client once every 8-hour shift if the skin remains intact.
Keep the client supine continuously for the first 24 postoperative hours.
Reposition only when the client requests a position change.

rationales.A: Correct. Frequent repositioning is the most important pressure-reduction factor; bed-confined clients should be turned at least every 2 hours with a written schedule to direct and document the turns.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waiting until every 8 hours is far less frequent than the minimum every-2-hour turning recommended for bed-confined clients.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Continuous supine positioning increases pressure-injury risk; early and scheduled repositioning is needed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. High-risk clients need a scheduled repositioning plan; relying only on client request is insufficient.

items.topic: Pressure injury prevention — repositioning schedule

sources.evidence: Frequent repositioning most important; written schedule; bed patients turned minimum every 2 hours.

items.stem: An adult with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Intravenous 0.9% saline has been started. The first serum potassium result is 3.0 mmol/L (3.0 mEq/L). Which action regarding insulin therapy is appropriate at this time?

options.text: Begin regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h IV immediately to correct the acidosis.
Withhold insulin temporarily, replace potassium, and start insulin once potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L.
Give subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin only; intravenous insulin is not used in adult DKA.
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate first; insulin is unnecessary if bicarbonate is corrected.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Starting insulin while potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L risks dangerous further hypokalemia because insulin drives potassium into cells.
rationales.B: Correct. If serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin is withheld (or stopped) while potassium is replaced until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L. Diabetes Canada also emphasizes fluid resuscitation, avoidance of hypokalemia, and insulin as core DKA principles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Adult DKA requires intravenous insulin (Diabetes Canada: 0.1 units/kg/h) for resolution; subcutaneous-only regimens are not the standard emergency approach described here.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is considered only for extreme acidosis (pH ≤7.0) and does not replace insulin therapy.

items.topic: DKA — withhold insulin if severe hypokalemia
items.jurisdiction_note: Diabetes Canada and Merck both prioritize potassium management with insulin in DKA; the <3.3 mmol/L hold threshold is stated explicitly in Merck.

items.stem: A client with heart failure takes digoxin daily and was recently started on furosemide. Which laboratory finding most increases the risk of digoxin toxicity?

options.text: Serum potassium 2.9 mmol/L (2.9 mEq/L)
Serum sodium 138 mmol/L (138 mEq/L)
Hemoglobin 128 g/L (12.8 g/dL)
Serum glucose 5.8 mmol/L (104 mg/dL)

rationales.A: Correct. Hypokalemia sensitizes the myocardium to digoxin so toxicity may occur even when the digoxin level is in the usual range. Potassium-depleting diuretics such as furosemide increase this risk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A sodium of 138 mmol/L is within a typical reference interval and is not the classic precipitant of digoxin toxicity highlighted in labelling.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hemoglobin near 128 g/L does not specifically increase digoxin toxicity risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A glucose of 5.8 mmol/L is not a recognized precipitant of digoxin toxicity in the cited sources.

items.topic: Digoxin — hypokalemia increases toxicity risk

items.stem: Before giving the morning digoxin tablet, the nurse counts the client's apical pulse for 1 full minute and obtains 52 beats/min. The client is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Administer the digoxin as scheduled because the client has no symptoms.
Withhold the digoxin and notify the health-care provider.
Give half the ordered dose and recheck the pulse in 30 minutes.
Crush the tablet and give it with a high-potassium food to prevent toxicity.

rationales.A: Incorrect. An apical rate under 60 beats/min is an indication to withhold digoxin pending provider guidance, even if the client currently feels well.
rationales.B: Correct. Nursing practice guidance is to assess the pulse for 1 minute and not administer digoxin if the heart rate is less than 60 beats/min. The Canadian monograph likewise notes that bradycardia related to digoxin may require temporary withdrawal and monitoring.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nurses do not independently halve digoxin doses; the dose should be withheld and the provider notified.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Crushing is not indicated solely for a low pulse, and giving the dose despite bradycardia is unsafe.

items.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin for stroke prevention. The nurse reinforces teaching about the usual therapeutic INR target range for this indication. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: My INR goal is usually about 2.0 to 3.0.
My INR should stay below 1.0 at all times.
An INR above 5.0 is ideal for preventing clots.
Warfarin does not require blood-test monitoring once I feel well.

rationales.A: Correct. For most treatment durations, including atrial fibrillation, the Canadian product monograph targets an INR of 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0). OpenStax likewise cites a usual therapeutic INR of about 2–3.
rationales.B: Incorrect. An INR near or below 1.0 reflects little anticoagulant effect and does not meet the therapeutic target for atrial fibrillation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Higher intensity anticoagulation increases bleeding risk; the monograph notes INR values greater than 4.0 provide little added benefit and raise bleeding risk for most patients.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Warfarin dosing is adjusted according to PT/INR results and requires ongoing monitoring.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after starting a packed red blood cell transfusion, a client reports chills and new flank pain. Temperature has risen from 36.8°C to 38.2°C. After the nurse stops the transfusion, which concurrent action is most appropriate?

Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing, and notify the blood bank.
Restart the same unit at a slower rate after giving acetaminophen.

items.stem: A postoperative client has brisk wound drainage into a surgical drain. The client is anxious. Capillary refill is delayed, skin is cool and clammy, heart rate is 118 beats/min, and blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg. Which interpretation best fits these findings?

options.text: Early compensatory response to hypovolemia; tachycardia can precede frank hypotension.
Cardiogenic shock is most likely because blood pressure is still near the client's baseline.
Findings are reassuring; hypovolemic shock is excluded until systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mm Hg.
Neurogenic shock is most likely because the client is anxious after surgery.

rationales.A: Correct. In early hypovolemic compensation, sympathetic activation raises heart rate and vascular tone; blood pressure may remain normal or only slightly changed while tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and anxiety appear.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock involves pump failure; this picture of volume loss with compensatory tachycardia fits hypovolemia, not a primary cardiac pump problem.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypotension is common in shock but is not required early; clients may be normotensive while compensation is still effective.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neurogenic shock typically features bradycardia and warm dry skin from loss of sympathetic tone, not compensatory tachycardia with cool clammy skin.

items.stem: A client receiving a loop diuretic reports new muscle weakness and cramps. Serum potassium is 2.7 mmol/L (2.7 mEq/L). Which nursing action is the priority?

rationales.C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase urinary potassium loss and would worsen hypokalemia; the diuretic should not be given until the provider reassesses.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dietary potassium is usually increased, not withheld, when treating hypokalemia unless the provider directs otherwise.

items.stem: A hospitalized adult with decreased level of consciousness is at risk for aspiration. Which nursing action best reduces aspiration risk during care?

options.text: Keep the client flat in a fully supine position for all oral care and feeding attempts.
Elevate the head of the bed to greater than 30 degrees (semi-upright) unless contraindicated, and avoid oral intake while consciousness is decreased.

items.stem: An immobile client after a stroke has flaccid extremities and cannot participate in active exercise. Which nursing intervention best helps prevent joint contractures?

Ask the spouse to override the client’s refusal and sign consent.

items.stem: Which nursing action is the most effective strategy to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) in a hospitalized adult?

Avoid unnecessary catheterization and remove the indwelling catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.

items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 6.4 mmol/L (6.4 mEq/L). Which electrocardiogram (ECG) change is most consistent with hyperkalemia?

Shortened PR interval with no T-wave changes

items.stem: An immobile hospitalized adult is at high risk for pressure injury. Which nursing intervention best reduces pressure-related tissue injury risk?

Contact Precautions only, because measles never spreads through the air.

items.stem: Under Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act and CNO Consent guidance, which statement about decision-making capacity is accurate?

Only a court can ever determine that a person is capable of consenting to treatment.

items.stem: An 82-year-old client living in a retirement residence develops new confusion over 12 hours without reported dysuria. Which nursing interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Acute confusion in an older adult can be an atypical presentation of urinary tract infection and warrants prompt clinical evaluation (including urine testing as indicated)
New delirium in older adults is almost never related to infection, so infection workup can be deferred indefinitely
UTI in older adults always presents with classic dysuria and frequency, so absent dysuria rules out UTI
Confusion should be attributed only to dementia progression without assessing acute medical causes

rationales.B: Incorrect. Infection (including UTI) is a common precipitant of delirium (Merck Delirium etiology; OpenStax).
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax and Merck emphasize atypical presentations without classic dysuria.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Acute confusion requires evaluation for reversible causes such as infection (OpenStax/Merck).

items.stem: A client arrives after prolonged outdoor cold exposure with a numb, pale finger. Which initial rewarming approach is most appropriate if medical care is arranged and refreezing will not occur?

options.text: Immerse the frostbitten area in warm (about 37–39 °C / warm-to-touch, not hot) water; do not rub or massage the area
Rub snow vigorously onto the finger to ‘restore circulation’
Place the numb finger directly on a stove burner or heating pad for rapid dry heat
Ignore the finding because numbness means tissue injury cannot occur

rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: avoid uncontrolled dry heat (stove, heating pad) because numbness risks burns.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Numbness is a classic frostbite finding and needs care (CDC/Merck).

conditions.text: Isolated anxiety attack without cold exposure

actions.text: Move to a warm shelter and arrange prompt medical evaluation
Rewarm the affected part in warm (≈37–39 °C / warm-to-touch) water without rubbing

Apply a heating pad directly to the numb skin for rapid dry heat

items.stem: A client with known primary adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, abdominal pain, and hypotension after a gastrointestinal illness. Which action is the immediate priority?

options.text: Recognize possible adrenal crisis and ensure emergency glucocorticoid therapy (e.g., IV hydrocortisone) with fluid resuscitation is instituted without delay
Withhold all steroids indefinitely because illness means hormones are unnecessary
Focus only on outpatient scheduling of elective imaging before any hormone replacement
Give a large dose of insulin as first-line therapy for adrenal crisis

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: institute therapy immediately on suspicion of adrenal crisis; delay in glucocorticoid therapy may be fatal; hydrocortisone IV and volume expansion. OpenStax: adrenal crisis treated with IV fluids, dextrose, and hydrocortisone; emergency—notify provider immediately.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Illness/stress increases glucocorticoid need; abrupt inadequate dosing precipitates crisis (OpenStax/Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Emergency hormone/fluid therapy precedes elective diagnostics (Merck: do not delay treatment).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Insulin is not first-line adrenal crisis therapy; hydrocortisone and fluids are.

items.stem: An Ontario client in independent nursing practice asks to discontinue nursing services. According to CNO accountabilities, which action is required?

options.text: Arrange timely alternative or replacement services, or give the client a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternative services
Stop all contact immediately without arranging or allowing time for alternative care
Refuse the client’s request and continue visits indefinitely regardless of the client’s wishes
Transfer the client’s health records to social media so the public can find another nurse

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code of Conduct 3.13 and the Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care standard: when services are discontinued at the client’s request, nurses arrange timely alternative or replacement services or provide a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternatives. Professional misconduct rules likewise require alternatives or a reasonable opportunity unless the client requests discontinuation (which still requires ensuring ongoing access).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Abrupt cessation without arranging alternatives or a reasonable opportunity abandons needed care and conflicts with CNO continuity accountabilities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Capable clients may request discontinuation; nurses must respect the request while ensuring ongoing access pathways (CNO).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sharing PHI on social media violates privacy and is not an alternative-care arrangement.

items.stem: A home-care client asks the nurse to borrow $50 until the next pension cheque. Which response best upholds professional boundaries?

options.text: Decline financial transactions unrelated to care (do not lend or borrow money) and, if needed, refer the client to appropriate resources
Lend the money from personal funds because the amount is small and the client seems trustworthy
Ask the client to add the nurse as a joint bank-account holder to ‘help manage bills’

items.stem: A nurse slept only 3 hours before a busy shift and feels less sharp than usual. Using the TeamSTEPPS I’M SAFE checklist, which action best supports situation monitoring?

Hide the fatigue and refuse any help so no one questions competence

items.stem: A 4-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, remains eager to feed, and has a palpable olive-like epigastric mass. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

actions.text: Support airway/breathing as needed and keep NPO pending surgical evaluation
Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with IV fluids as ordered before surgery
Encourage unlimited formula immediately before emergent laparotomy without fluid resuscitation
Prepare for pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization as ordered
Discharge home without evaluation because vomiting is always normal at this age

parameters.text: Hydration status and urine output
Serum electrolytes (watch for hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis)
Stock market indices
Unrelated school grades of siblings
Weight trend / ongoing vomiting frequency

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not produce an olive-like pyloric mass with classic projectile nonbilious pattern of IHPS.
rationales.K2: Correct. Merck/NCBI: IHPS — projectile nonbilious vomiting in early weeks with possible olive mass.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Appendicitis is not the classic 3–6 week olive-mass presentation.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Progressive projectile vomiting with olive mass is not simple overfeeding.
rationales.A1: Incorrect. While NPO pending evaluation may occur, the sourced priority actions are fluid/electrolyte correction and pyloromyotomy after stabilization.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: correct dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities before pyloromyotomy.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Feeding without correcting fluids/electrolytes and rushing without stabilization is unsafe.
rationales.A4: Correct. Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.A5: Incorrect. This presentation requires prompt evaluation, not casual discharge.
rationales.P1: Correct. Dehydration risk is central; monitor hydration/urine output (Merck).
rationales.P2: Correct. Classic abnormality is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.P5: Plausible monitoring but not selected as a keyed parameter for this item; electrolytes and hydration are the highest-yield sourced parameters.

conditions.text: Typical slow-onset Alzheimer dementia as the sole explanation
Delirium (acute confusional state), often secondary to acute illness
Stable lifelong intellectual disability without acute change

Provide a calm supportive environment; avoid restraints when possible
Assume the change is permanent dementia and cancel medical workup

rationales.P1: Correct. Track mental status/attention and fluctuation (core delirium features).

items.topic: NGN bowtie — myxedema coma: IV thyroid hormone + glucocorticoids; hypothermia/respiratory depression

conditions.text: Adrenal crisis from abrupt steroid withdrawal only

actions.text: Administer intravenous thyroid hormone (T4/T3) as ordered
Give glucocorticoids as ordered while adrenal insufficiency is not yet excluded
Rapidly rewarm with aggressive external heating to reverse hypotension
Start high-dose oral methimazole immediately as first-line therapy
Encourage ambulation without airway or temperature support

rationales.P2: Correct. Respiratory depression/CO2 retention and hypoxemia require ventilation/PaO2 monitoring (Merck/OpenStax).

items.topic: IV infiltration — cool swollen site; stop infusion and remove catheter

Ignore the findings if the pump is not alarming

items.topic: Acute mania — calm clear communication; do not challenge grandiosity; prioritize safety

Encourage a large stimulating group activity to burn off energy

items.topic: NGN bowtie — acute dystonia from antipsychotic: recognize and treat with benztropine/diphenhydramine
items.stem: A client who recently started a first-generation antipsychotic develops sudden torticollis and tongue spasms. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Tardive dyskinesia only (late irreversible choreiform movements)

actions.text: Notify the provider and administer benztropine or diphenhydramine as ordered (IV/IM)
Hold further doses of the causative antipsychotic pending provider guidance
Encourage the client to ignore the spasms and continue the same antipsychotic dose without assessment
Start a high-dose SSRI immediately as first-line therapy for the spasms
Force oral intake of a large high-carbohydrate meal as the only intervention

parameters.text: Airway patency and ability to swallow/speak (watch for laryngeal involvement)
Resolution of muscle spasms / dystonic movements after treatment
Peak expiratory flow only as the sole monitoring plan
Urine specific gravity every minute without neuromuscular assessment
Orthostatic blood pressure after sprint exercise only

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect, not the acute spasmodic torticollis/tongue spasm picture.
rationales.K2: Correct. OpenStax: dystonia includes spasms of tongue, back, legs, neck — an EPS of antipsychotics. Merck: acute dystonic reactions (e.g., torticollis, oculogyric crisis).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: treat acute dystonia with benztropine IV/IM or diphenhydramine IV/IM.
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: monitor EPS so treatment can be given and antipsychotic regimen adjusted/changed.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Acute dystonia requires prompt treatment.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. SSRIs are not treatment for dystonia.
rationales.P1: Correct. Merck notes laryngeal dystonia may threaten airway.
rationales.P2: Correct. Reassess spasm resolution after anticholinergic/antihistamine therapy.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Peak flow alone misses airway/neuromuscular priorities.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Not priority monitoring for acute dystonia.

items.topic: Ontario consent — capacity is treatment-specific; capable client decides
items.stem: An Ontario nurse reviews consent for two different procedures proposed for the same client. Which statement reflects CNO/HCCA capacity principles?

options.text: Capacity is treatment-specific — a client may be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if capable, the client decides
Once found incapable for any decision, the client is permanently incapable for all future treatments
Nurses may independently override a capable client’s refusal whenever the nurse disagrees
A family member may consent for a clearly capable adult who refuses treatment

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Consent: capacity relates to a specific treatment; a person could be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if the client is capable, the client makes the decision.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Capacity is decision/treatment-specific and can change.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Practitioners lack authority to decide for capable clients except limited emergencies.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Capable clients decide for themselves; SDM is used when the client is incapable.
